intro.html: Some people hold their ground; some give way. English has a crowd of words for the first kind, and the trick is that they do not all mean the same thing about the person. Holding on to a goal through every setback is tenacious or steadfast, and we admire it. Refusing to budge when you are plainly wrong is obstinate or obdurate, and we don’t.

Ask two questions about each word: Is the person firm or yielding? and Does the writer approve? Resolute and steadfast praise firmness; intransigent and recalcitrant blame it. At the other end, docile and malleable describe someone (or something) easy to lead or shape.
Several of these words carry pictures inside them. Recalcitrant comes from a Latin verb for kicking back with the heels, obdurate from a verb for hardening, and malleable from the Latin for hammer.

words.def: stubbornly refusing to change one’s mind or plan
words.ex: The {obstinate} toddler refused to wear anything but her rain boots, even on a sunny day.
words.ctx: Everyone else agreed the trail was washed out, but Uncle Victor was {obstinate}; he insisted on hiking it anyway and came back two hours later, muddy to the knees.
words.etym: From Latin obstinatus, “determined,” from obstinare (to persist): ob- (in the way) + a part akin to stare (to stand).

mn.text: The donkey stands in the middle of the gate, and no amount of pushing will move it: it is {obstinate}.

scene.alt: A man pushes and pushes a grumpy donkey that will not move from the gate.

words.def: holding on firmly; refusing to give up
words.ex: The {tenacious} terrier would not let go of the rope toy.
words.ctx: Most reporters gave up after the mayor’s office ignored their calls, but one {tenacious} young writer kept asking questions for months until she got answers.
words.etym: From Latin tenax, “holding fast,” from tenere (to hold).

mn.cue: holds on with all TEN fingers
mn.text: The wind howls around the cliff, but Maya holds on with all ten fingers and keeps climbing: she is {tenacious}.

scene.alt: A climber clings to a big rock in the wind and keeps reaching higher.

words.def: firm and loyal; not changing or giving way
words.ex: Through every losing season, the team’s {steadfast} fans filled the bleachers.
words.ctx: Friends came and went over the years, but Lila remained {steadfast}; whenever Rosa needed help, Lila was the first to show up.
words.etym: From Old English stedefæst, “fixed in its place”: stede (place) + fæst (fixed, firm).

mn.cue: STEADY, held FAST in its place
mn.text: Every stormy night, keeper Tia stays at her post and keeps the lighthouse lamp burning for the boats: she is {steadfast}.

scene.alt: On a stormy night, a lighthouse keeper in a raincoat holds up a lantern, staying at her post.

words.def: firmly insisting; refusing to be talked out of something
words.ex: Grandpa was {adamant} that we wear our seat belts, even for a one-block drive.
words.ctx: The class begged for one more week to finish their projects, but the teacher was {adamant}: the deadline was Friday, and no pleading would change it.
words.etym: From an old noun adamant, a stone once believed to be unbreakable, from Greek adamas, “unconquerable.”

mn.cue: a NO as hard as a DIAMOND
mn.text: Pip begs to have cake for breakfast, but Granny Mae’s “no” is as hard as a diamond: she is {adamant}. (Diamond and adamant come from the same Greek word, adamas.)

scene.alt: A boy begs on his knees while his grandmother crosses her arms and says no; a hard diamond shines above her.

words.def: firmly determined; set on a purpose
words.ex: With a {resolute} face, Dev stepped up to take the last penalty kick.
words.ctx: The flood had ruined half the town’s shops, yet the owners were {resolute}; within a month they had cleaned, repaired and reopened every door on Main Street.
words.etym: From Latin resolutus, past participle of resolvere (to loosen, settle).

mn.cue: REZ-uh-LOOT: won’t quit till the LOOT
mn.text: Captain Ada has dug for three days, and she won’t stop until she finds the loot: she is {resolute}.

labels.text: RESO-LOOT: till I find the LOOT

scene.alt: A determined pirate digs on a sandy island toward a buried treasure chest.

words.def: refusing to compromise or give way at all
words.ex: The two {intransigent} cats each refused to give up the sunny spot on the porch.
words.ctx: The talks failed because both sides were {intransigent}: neither would give up a single demand, so the meeting ended without even a partial deal.
words.etym: From Spanish intransigente, “not coming to an agreement,” from Latin in- (not) + transigere (to come to terms).

mn.cue: the GENT who won’t make a deal: in-TRANS-i-GENT
mn.text: Pip offers nine coins for the hat, then nine and a half, but the seller is a gent who will not bend an inch: “Ten, or no deal.” He is {intransigent}.

scene.alt: A boy offers coins for a hat, but the seller crosses his arms and will not lower his price.

words.def: stubbornly refusing to obey or cooperate
words.ex: The {recalcitrant} printer jammed every time we tried to print the poster.
words.ctx: Most of the campers lined up when the whistle blew, but a few {recalcitrant} boys stayed on the dock and ignored every call to come in.
words.etym: From Latin recalcitrare, “to kick back with the heels”: re- (back) + calx (heel).

mn.cue: KICKS BACK with his heels: re-CALC-itrant
mn.text: At bath time, Theo kicks his heels and shouts “No!” He fights every rule: he is {recalcitrant}.

scene.alt: A toddler sits on the floor kicking his heels and shouting no while his mother waits with the soap.

words.def: hard-hearted and stubborn, especially when one should give way
words.ex: Even the puppy’s sad eyes could not soften the {obdurate} landlord.
words.ctx: The children explained, apologized and offered to pay for the window, but the neighbor remained {obdurate}, refusing even to listen.
words.etym: From Latin obdurare, “to harden,” from durus (hard).

mn.text: However nicely the children ask, Rex won’t give back the ball that flew over his fence; his heart is as hard as durable stone. He is {obdurate}.

scene.alt: Two sad children ask for their ball back across a fence, but a grumpy man holds it up and refuses.

words.def: calm and easy to teach, lead or control
words.ex: The {docile} old horse let every child at the fair take a turn on its back.
words.ctx: The trainer warned that the puppy would not stay {docile} forever; once it was bigger, it would pull hard on the leash unless it learned to heel now.
words.etym: From Latin docilis, “easily taught,” from docere (to teach).

mn.cue: DOS-ul: it DOES ALL you ask
mn.text: Ask the pony to walk, stop or turn, and it does all you ask: it is {docile}.

scene.alt: A girl leads a calm, happy pony that follows her wherever she goes.

words.def: easily shaped or bent; also, easily influenced
words.ex: Warm wax is {malleable}, so the children pressed it into star shapes.
words.ctx: Young children’s tastes are {malleable}; a toddler who hates peas this month may ask for seconds next month after seeing an older cousin enjoy them.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin malleabilis, from malleare (to hammer), from malleus (hammer).

mn.text: A few taps of the smith’s mallet and the soft gold bends into a ring: gold is {malleable}.

scene.alt: A smith taps soft gold with a mallet, shaping it into a ring.

head: firm, and the writer approves
firm, and the writer disapproves
yielding
rows: tenacious: holds on, won’t give up
obstinate: won’t change a bad plan
malleable: easy to shape or sway
after.cap: The same firmness can be praise or blame. Look for the writer’s attitude in the sentence.

after.html: A writer who likes a stubborn character calls her tenacious or resolute; a writer who doesn’t calls her obstinate. On a test, read the sentence around the blank: if the stubbornness is causing trouble (“refused to listen,” “made things worse”), choose a word that blames.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: Her {tenacious} effort finally paid off: after forty tries, the kite flew.

after.cap: The effort paid off, so the writer approves: tenacious.

items.q: After forty failed tries, Zoe finally got her kite to fly. The writer admires her. Which word fits best?
items.why: Tenacious praises someone who holds on and won’t give up. Obstinate and recalcitrant are firm too, but they blame the person.

items.q: Even after the map showed he was lost, Grandpa refused to ask for directions, and the trip took three extra hours. Grandpa was…
items.why: His firmness caused trouble, so the writer is blaming him: obstinate. Steadfast and resolute are words of praise.

items.q: True or false: docile is an opposite of recalcitrant.
items.why: True. A docile animal or person is easy to lead; a recalcitrant one stubbornly refuses to obey.

items.q: Which sentence uses malleable in its “easily influenced” sense?
choices: His opinions were malleable: whoever spoke last could change his mind.
The copper sheet was malleable enough to bend by hand.
The malleable clay took the shape of the bowl.
items.why: Malleable first meant able to be hammered into shape (copper, clay); it also describes people or ideas that are easily shaped by others.
